characterInteraction.description: Elif Shafak leads the conversation, engaging with the other attendees through her speech and gestures. The other attendees listen attentively, occasionally nodding or drinking water. Some smile in response to Elif's points.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Discussion on the complexities of identity and the impact of globalization and humanism.

narrativeProgression.description: Elif Shafak starts talking about how cultures use narratives to tell us who we are through simplification.
Elif mentions how people are told they can only have one primary identity.
Elif talks about how extremist ideologies simplify complexity and are based on exclusionary identity politics.
Elif expresses her problems with organized religions due to their "us vs them" mentality.
Elif acknowledges that intellectuals and liberals haven't done a good job in connecting with people's anxieties.
Elif emphasizes the need to resist simplifying things and embrace the complexity of human beings.
Elif argues that multiple belongings increase the chance of finding common ground.
Elif highlights the importance of abolishing exclusionary identity politics.
Elif stresses the need for a more radical humanism.
Elif calls for open conversations about neglected subjects like faith and doubt.
Elif argues that sameness won't bring safety in our globalized world.

scenes.thematicElements: Identity politics, Humanism, Globalization, Faith and Doubt

climax.description: Elif highlights the importance of abolishing exclusionary identity politics.

storylines.description: The video explores the dangers of simplification and exclusionary identity politics, advocating for a broader understanding and embracing of complexity.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: We grow up in cultures with narratives that tell us who we are by ways of simplification.
And this is happening everywhere.
So I am being told that if you are coming from a Muslim geography, you are a Muslim and
you can be nothing else or this has to be your primary identity.
If you go elsewhere, you will come across the same narrative across Europe from the far
right.
If you are a Christian or if you are a Dutch, just be that and nothing else.
All the extreme ideologies what they have in common is they simplify complexity.
And they are based on identity politics and all identity politics is based on exclusion.
That's why I have a huge problem with all kinds of organized religions because they are
based on a distinction between us versus them and the presumption that us is better than
them.
Sometimes they express, sometimes not expressed.
So I do agree that we intellectuals or the left, the liberals have not done a very good
job in terms of connecting with people's anxieties and we must be critical of that.
But at the same time we have to see, we have to resist this tendency to simplify things.
Because as human beings we are so complex, we are composed of multiple selves.
We are made of water.
Our main element is water.
It's based on flow.
What do I mean is, yes, I'm an Istanbulite, I'm at the same time a Londoner, I have connections
to the Balkans, I have connections to the Middle East.
There is in me so many elements from the Middle East, you know.
At the same time I'm a European by choice, at the same time I'm a world citizen, at the
same time I'm a global soul.
So if I can have multiple, multiple belongings, there's a bigger chance that my multiple
belongings will converge with yours.
But if I am based defined on the basis of a single, exclusivist identity politics, there's
no way we can find common ground.
We need to abolish that narrative that tells us, you can only be one thing.
You can only, you know, simplify the narrative.
And for that we need intellectuals.
We need to go back to human beings.
We need to go back to the basics, but revolutionize it, radicalize it.
We can have a more radical humanism.
And I know I spoke, you know, I'm taking your time, but if I may add this, we need to also
talk about certain subjects that we have abandoned for too long.
And faith is one of them.
I think faith is a subject that's too important to abandon to the religious.
You know, and faith is not necessarily a religious concept.
When you start writing a book, it's an act of faith.
When you fall in love, it's an act of faith.
When you move to a new city, it's an act of faith.
There's so many moments in our lives that are acts of faith that have nothing to do with
religion.
And we also need doubt, because faith without doubt will turn into dogma.
So we need the vaults.
We need the dance, the dialectics of faith and that.
These are also issues that we don't talk about.
And if we don't talk about these things, people go to the far right, people go to the religious
because the reason need to talk about these issues.
We are being pulled into very opposite directions.
And the second trend is gaining speed right now.
Yes, on the one hand, we had high hopes, you know, about world citizens, global souls,
internationalism, multiculturalism, which is not a favorable word anymore.
And then the other one, the tribalism, isolationism, the illusion that sameness will bring safety.
This is what we are being spoon-fed right now.
They're telling us if you are being surrounded by people who are exactly like you, who dress
up like you, speak like you, who come from the same background.
You'll be safe.
It's an illusion.
We are far too globalized to have this.
Whether we have walls, actual physical walls or not, sameness will not bring us safety.
